verses.translation_literal: Praise Yah! I will give thanks [to] YHWH with all [my] heart, in the council of the upright and [the] congregation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hallelu-Yah! Lift your voices — for I will lift mine. With the whole of my heart, holding nothing back, I will give thanks to the LORD, here among the upright, where the counsel is kept, and before the whole gathered congregation.
verses.directors_commentary:
The opening cry is the plural command 'Halelu' (you all, praise) plus the short divine name Yah. The singer first calls the room to worship, then commits himself: 'I will give thanks.' Then the poem begins its machinery. Every half-line from here to the end opens with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, aleph in 'I will give thanks' (אוֹדֶה), bet in 'in the council' (בְּסוֹד), and so on to the final tav. Nothing of this survives in the KJV, and it matters: the psalm is built to be learned by heart, a memory-ladder for a congregation.

The KJV renders both hallel and yadah as 'praise', losing the difference between exuberant praise and thanksgiving that confesses what God has done. It also gives 'assembly' for sod, which is a smaller thing: the intimate circle of counsel, those who are in on a matter (the same word is used for a confidential conversation). So the staging is two circles: the inner company of the upright, and the wider congregation. Play it as a man speaking first to friends, then standing to address the whole village.

philological_notes.note: 'In the council of'. Sod is a close circle of counsel or confidence, narrower than 'edah, the whole congregation. Metzudat Zion links it to a counsel made in secret, or to yesod, 'foundation'. The two nouns together give an inner circle and an outer one.

A plural imperative, 'you all praise', with the short form of the divine name. It stands outside the acrostic. Rashi notes that the psalm itself is alphabetic, with one letter at the head of the verse and one in its middle.

verses.translation_literal: Great [are] the works of YHWH, sought out for all their delights.
verses.translation_dramatic: Great are the works of the LORD, great and open to the searching. Whoever delights in them goes looking, and finds that every one of them was made to be sought out.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two words carry the verse. Darush, 'sought out', is the verb of study and enquiry (the later word midrash comes from the same root). The works of God are not merely admired, they are investigated, and the psalm assumes that the investigator is rewarded. The KJV's 'sought out of all them that have pleasure therein' is faithful but archaic: 'of' means 'by'.

The second is the Hebrew's last word, chefts-eihem, 'their delights', which can be read two ways: the delight those who study the works take in them (KJV, Ibn Ezra's 'those who delight') or the purposes built into the works, the reasons each one exists (Malbim: every work has its chefets, as a house is for dwelling in). The Hebrew keeps both open, and the actor should not choose. The letters now are gimel and dalet: 'Great' and 'sought out'.

philological_notes.note: 'Sought out, studied'. The root is the verb of enquiry, including the study of Scripture. The works of God are an object of research, and the search is assumed to succeed.

'Their delights'. Read either as 'those who delight in them' (Ibn Ezra and Radak) or as the purposes that each work serves (Malbim). Ibn Ezra explains the form as a plural with a suffix like zekenehem, 'their elders'.

verses.translation_literal: Splendor and majesty [is] his work, and his righteousness [is] standing for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: Splendor and majesty: that is his work. And his righteousness stands, immovable, for ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
The acrostic letters are he and vav, and the Hebrew gives the verse a rhyme in -o ('po'olo', 'tsidqato'), a sound the congregation would hear at each line's end. 'Hod wehadar' is royal vocabulary: honor and majesty are what clothes a king, and the words recur for God as monarch. The KJV's 'honourable and glorious' turns two nouns into adjectives and loses the picture of a robe of splendor.

The second line sets two verbs of standing against each other. God's righteousness 'stands' (omedet), and the psalm uses the same participle again in verse 10 for his praise. Righteousness here is not abstract virtue: tsedaqah is what God does for his people, the saving acts the psalm goes on to list. Malbim reads it as the unchanging order, in contrast to wonders, which come and go.

philological_notes.note: 'Splendor and majesty', the pair that describes a king's presence. Malbim distinguishes hod as the inner and hadar as the outward glory.

verses.translation_literal: A memorial he has made for his wonders; gracious and compassionate [is] YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: He has made a memorial of his wonders, so that they will not be lost. Gracious, and full of compassion — that is the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
Zayin and chet. The first line has no verb of remembering for God: it is God who 'makes a zeker', a memorial, a thing set up so that people remember. Rashi hears the festivals and Sabbaths ('you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt'), and Metzudat David the jar of manna kept for later generations. The KJV's 'hath made his wonderful works to be remembered' turns a noun into a purpose clause and loses the monument.

The second line is the great creed of Exodus 34:6, 'gracious and compassionate', here with the order of the names inverted and the divine name left until last, so it is the final word spoken. Ibn Ezra ties the line to God's hearing the cry of the oppressed. Where the KJV says 'full of compassion', the Hebrew has only the two adjectives; 'full of' is the translators' addition.

philological_notes.note: 'Gracious and compassionate', the formula from the revelation of the name in Exodus 34:6. Ibn Ezra compares Exodus 22:26, 'I will hear, for I am gracious'.
'A memorial, a remembrance': a thing made, which later generations use to remember. Rashi reads Sabbaths and festivals, Metzudat David the manna jar.

verses.translation_literal: Prey he has given to those who fear him; he remembers for ever his covenant.
verses.translation_dramatic: He has given prey to those who fear him, and what he gives he does not take back: for ever he remembers his covenant.
verses.directors_commentary:
Tet and yod. The surprise is the first word, teref. It is the word for what a lion tears: prey, the kill. The KJV's 'meat' and ASV's 'food' tame it. Psalm 111 has chosen a word with teeth, and the ancient commentators felt it: Metzudat Zion notes that it is 'borrowed from the food of a beast of prey', and Malbim follows the image, that Israel received the spoil of the peoples. Ibn Ezra and Radak hear the plunder carried out of Egypt; Metzudat David the manna in the desert. An actor can play it either way, as bread or as booty, but the word stays rough.

The second line is the answer to the first: he gives, and he remembers. 'The fear of him' is the posture of those who keep the covenant. The verb yizkor, 'he remembers', turns the human memorial of verse 4 around: now it is God who keeps the memory, for ever, of the promise to the fathers (Radak: the covenant between the pieces, Genesis 15).

philological_notes.note: 'Prey, torn food'. Usually the kill of a predator (Gen 49:27, of Benjamin); in Proverbs 31:15 and Malachi 3:10 it is household food. Here it keeps its wild edge, which is why the commentators read it as plunder.

verses.translation_literal: The power of his works he has declared to his people, to give to them an inheritance of nations.
verses.translation_dramatic: The power of his deeds he made known to his people, for he was giving them the inheritance of the nations.
verses.directors_commentary:
Kaf and lamed. The verse is about the conquest of Canaan, spoken as an old song. 'Nachalat goyim', 'the inheritance of nations': the land that the nations lived in becomes Israel's inherited property. The KJV's 'heathen' reads a later religious meaning into goyim; the Hebrew says 'nations', neutral and political. It also turns the infinitive 'to give' into 'that he may give', a purpose it does not state.

The verb is higgid, 'he declared, told'. God did not only act, he told his people the power of his acts. Radak sees that God announced the gift before he made it, so that it should not look like chance. Rashi, quoting Tanchuma, finds a theological answer to the charge of robbery: Genesis was written to show that the whole earth belongs to the Creator, who may settle on it whom he will. The psalm gives the claim in its first-audience form, as a thing God announced.

philological_notes.note: 'An inheritance of nations': land held as hereditary property, taken from the peoples who held it. 'Goyim' is neutral, 'nations', not 'heathen'.
'He declared, told': a causative verb of announcement. Radak notes that the telling came before the deed.

verses.translation_literal: The works of his hands [are] truth and justice; faithful [are] all his precepts.
verses.translation_dramatic: The works of his hands are truth and justice, and every one of his precepts can be trusted.
verses.directors_commentary:
Mem and nun. 'The works of his hands' is concrete: hands that act. The two nouns 'emet and mishpat, 'truth' and 'justice', are the standard of kingship. The KJV's 'verity and judgment' is accurate in the old sense but sounds as if 'judgment' were a verdict; mishpat is the right order that a just ruler establishes. Radak and Metzudat David both read the line against the conquest: driving out the nations was true, because it kept the promise to Abraham, and just, because of their wrongdoing.

The second line rests on the root 'amen. 'Emet' (truth), and 'ne'emanim' (faithful, reliable) belong to the same root, and the Hebrew makes the sound audible. 'Piqqudim', here 'precepts', is a favorite word of Psalm 119; it means what is appointed or commissioned, more than 'commandments' in the KJV. Ibn Ezra reads them as the law written on every heart.

philological_notes.note: 'His precepts, charges': what is appointed or commissioned. Close to 'commandments' but more administrative, rooted in the verb 'to appoint, to visit, to muster'.
'Faithful, reliable'. The same root as 'emet in the line before; a sound pair heard in the Hebrew only.

verses.translation_literal: Supported for ever [and] ever, made in truth and uprightness.
verses.translation_dramatic: They stand propped up for ever and ever, made in truth and in uprightness.
verses.directors_commentary:
Samekh and ayin. The verb is 'semukhim', 'supported, propped', as a building is held by pillars. Rashi pictures a structure: the precepts are held together 'like pillars', and he quotes Song of Songs 5:15, 'his legs are pillars of marble'. KJV's 'stand fast' is true to the meaning but loses the picture of something that rests on something else. Radak: they cannot fall, because they were made in truth and uprightness, so no one who follows them stumbles.

The doubled 'la'ad le'olam' is emphatic, 'for ever, to eternity'; the KJV's 'for ever and ever' keeps that. The second line returns to the verb of making ('asuyim), the same root (עשה) as 'works' (ma'aseh) in verses 2, 6 and 7: whatever God made is made in 'emet. (The po'al, 'work', of verse 3 is a different root, פעל, with a similar meaning.) The same word 'emet' returns from verse 7, 'yashar' (upright) from the opening verse; the poem closes its circle.

philological_notes.note: 'Supported, propped, held up'. Rashi relates it to a supporting pillar and quotes Song 5:15; Metzudat David reads 'resting on, relying on', so that the precepts have a foundation that cannot be removed.

verses.translation_literal: Redemption he sent to his people; he ordained for ever his covenant; holy and awesome [is] his name.
verses.translation_dramatic: Redemption he sent to his people. He laid down his covenant for ever. Holy is his name, and to be feared.
verses.directors_commentary:
Pe, tsade, qof: the three-letter line, as the poem's last two verses are longer. This is the Exodus verse: the sending of 'peduth', the price paid to buy back a person or property, a word of the slave market. The KJV's 'redemption' keeps the meaning. 'Shalach', 'he sent', is the verb of dispatching a messenger, so redemption is pictured as an envoy sent out. The verb is a past tense, but Meiri hears the future in it: the same God will send redemption again.

Tsivvah, 'he ordained' or 'commanded', is the verb of the covenant: KJV's 'commanded his covenant' is literal, but the psalm treats a covenant as something imposed, a charge, as well as made. Metzudat David ties it to the Torah given with the covenant, and Malbim says the redemption depended on keeping the precepts. The last line closes on the name. Nora' is 'to be feared', a passive: the name inspires awe, 'reverend' in the KJV is archaic and means a title for clergy to the modern ear. Say it with a hush.

philological_notes.note: 'Redemption, ransom': the buying back of a person or thing from another's claim; a word from the slave market and from the law of the firstborn. Metzudat David reads the redemption from Egypt.
'To be feared, awesome': a niphal participle of yr', the root of 'fear' in verses 5 and 10. The fear of the name closes the psalm's theme before verse 10 states it.

verses.translation_literal: The beginning of wisdom [is] the fear of YHWH; good understanding [belongs] to all who do them; his praise [is] standing for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the LORD. Good understanding is theirs who do them — and his praise stands for ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
Resh, shin, tav: three lines, the alphabet's end. After nine verses of what God has done, the psalm turns to what the hearer should do, and ends on the line that Proverbs 9:10 and Job 28:28 also use. 'Reshith' is 'beginning' in both senses, starting point and best part (BBE's 'the best part of wisdom' takes the second sense). The fear of YHWH is where wisdom starts, and Radak and Metzudat David both hold that it must come before the study of wisdom, never after.

The KJV's 'a good understanding have all they that do his commandments' adds 'his commandments': the Hebrew has only 'those who do them' ('osehem), with a plural 'them' that points back, to the precepts of verse 7 (Malbim) or, in Ibn Ezra's report of R. Moshe, to wisdom and fear. Sekhel tov, 'good understanding', also means 'success': Radak allows both. The final line recalls verse 3: 'omedet la'ad, 'standing for ever'. Whose praise: God's, or the doer's? Ibn Ezra and Radak allow the second. Let the last line hang between them.

philological_notes.note: 'The beginning of wisdom': 'reshith' means both the first part and the chief part. Radak argues that the fear of YHWH must come first, since the study of wisdom without it risks denying the signs and wonders in Scripture.
'Good understanding, good insight', which can also mean success or good sense in action. Radak reads 'good insight and good providence', or success in this world and the next.
'Those who do them': the 'them' is plural, with no antecedent in the verse. Malbim takes the precepts of the preceding verses; Ibn Ezra reports R. Moshe, who takes wisdom and fear.
